svg.title: Slack apps: a bot token scoped by OAuth, and events you must acknowledge within three seconds
svg.desc: Installing a Slack app runs OAuth, which grants a bot token starting xoxb- that is limited to exactly the scopes you request, such as chat:write, commands, and channels:history; following least privilege you do not request broad admin scopes. When something happens, Slack's Events API POSTs the event to your endpoint and expects an HTTP 200 within three seconds. If you are too slow, Slack assumes failure and retries, delivering the event again, so a slow handler causes duplicate processing. The correct pattern is to acknowledge immediately with ack, then do the real work asynchronously in the background. A footer notes Socket Mode as an alternative that needs no public URL, and that requests should be verified using the signing secret.
svg.text: A token scoped to least privilege — and a 3-second clock on every event
OAuth: a token limited to its scopes
Bot token: xoxb-... (identifies the app)
chat:write · commands · channels:history
grant
admin · users:write · broad scopes
skip
Least privilege: a leaked token can do only what its scopes allow.
Events API: answer within 3 seconds
Slack POSTs an event
to your request URL
ack() → HTTP 200
immediately, < 3s
then do the real work asynchronously (queue / background task)
Too slow → Slack assumes failure & retries → duplicate delivery
Two ideas define Slack apps. First, scopes: OAuth hands your bot a token that can do only what you declared, so
request the minimum — every extra scope widens the blast radius if the token leaks. Second, the 3-second rule: the
Events API retries anything it thinks failed, so a handler that does slow work inline gets the same event two or three
times. Always ack() first, then process in the background, and make handlers idempotent so a retry is harmless.
Two ways to receive events
Events API (HTTP): Slack POSTs to your public URL — verify each request with the signing secret.
Socket Mode (WebSocket): your app dials out, so no public URL or inbound firewall hole — ideal for dev & internal bots.
